:class:`PatternCriterionModel`, with the anchoring inverted.

``content_conditions`` is non-empty by contract and ``tool_patterns`` is optional, the reverse of gate
#1. Each gate's anchor is the thing it exists to talk about — which action at a call, what came back at
a response — and the inversion is what lets one rule cover every tool the account has. Empty
``tool_patterns`` means *any tool*, which at gate #1 would be a rule its author never meant.

``variant`` is tagged distinctly (``response_pattern``) for the reason
:class:`ModelRequestPatternCriterionModel` is: all three are ``CriterionVariant.PATTERN`` underneath, so
the tag is what lets one discriminated union carry them and the *gate* is what decides which a guardrail
may hold.

while the gate is not in ``ENFORCED_GATES``, so nothing routes here on the way in — but ``GET``/``LIST``
must render a stored row created the sanctioned way, and rendering it as some other gate's shape is the
500 that #4560 fixed for ``model_request``.

whether ``eligible_domain`` is currently trusted (the toggle's state).

piece of declared config that stays operator-owned for *every* agent, including a catalog one:
it is a control-plane value chosen at deploy time, not behavior baked into the pinned image, so
the catalog-immutability rule that seals prompt/model/skills does not apply to it. Until this
existed the allowlist was write-once — set on deploy and unreachable afterwards — which left an
orchestrator unable to ever gain a specialist.

An empty list clears the allowlist, which means *unrestricted* (the whole fleet), not "none".

resume are their own routes so each is a distinct audited verb rather than a diff a reader has to

identity a customer names, so a patch says "these are the criteria now" rather than merging into a
list whose order and membership the caller cannot address.

``gate`` is deliberately absent, and stays absent now that a second gate is authorable: moving a rule
to another gate would keep criteria that mean nothing there, so the move is a delete and a rewrite, not
a patch. Criteria supplied here are checked against the gate the rule already stands at.

``kind`` is immutable after create and is absent here intentionally.
``envelope_version`` is the per-sink opt-in for a future envelope schema revision (§4
"Versioning"): every sink is created at version 1 and bumped explicitly when the sink operator
opts into a new envelope shape — no separate route.

``labels`` and ``allowlist`` replace wholesale when given rather than merging. A merge has no way to
express a *removal*, and an allowlist an operator cannot narrow is the wrong shape for a deny-by-
default list.

UpdateSelfHostedAgentConfigRequest.description:

step), so the next Edit pre-fills from this save rather than the original creation-time config.

**hosted** agent's config lives elsewhere (the GitOps values.yaml — use the hosted-agent routes),
and a **catalog** agent's behavior is baked into its pinned image, so no edit here could change it.
A draft (never reported in) still uses ``UpdateAgentDraftRequest``. The wizard always sends
the full config, so unlike that request's ``config`` this one is required, not optional.

``config`` is required and must be non-empty, and unknown top-level keys are rejected (``extra
="forbid"``): a malformed body (e.g. the config fields sent at the top level instead of wrapped in
``{"config": {...}}``) must 422, never silently persist an empty ``{}`` and wipe the agent's saved
declared config.

``mcp_group_id`` is not declared config — it is the column the platform reads, and it is
tri-state: omit it to leave the current binding alone, send ``null`` to unbind.

Operator-only (``require_user``): creating a worker token is an operator action; a worker token must not reach it.

Returns 200 when everything asked for was done, and 207 when the agent was created but a trigger
was not — never 200 for a trigger that does not exist.

207.description: The agent was created but at least one requested trigger was not — each entry in `triggers` says which, and carries the real error plus the endpoint that creates just that trigger. The agent and its worker token exist and the returned `command`/`values` are valid, so retry the TRIGGER, not this call: re-posting it rotates the worker token and invalidates a values.yaml already applied.

post.description:
How many agent versions were deployed in the window — the fleet's rate of change.

``window_days`` is calendar-day inclusive (``1`` is today alone), matching the run-activity
reads, so this tile and the ones beside it cover the same period. ``agent_ids`` behaves as on
the status route: omitted means account-wide, ``[]`` returns zero.

Counts every generation minted in the window, including an agent's first deploy and including a
dual-deploy shadow arm's generations — the ledger carries no arm column. A rollback counts once
the version it rolls back from has fully drained; while a replica still runs the old card the
generation is reused and nothing is written.

Declared before the ``/{agent_id}`` routes so the literal path wins.

Create (or resume) a *draft* agent for the Add-Agent wizard's first step.

Freezes an opaque agent_id against the friendly name so the wizard is resumable by id and the
eventual worker token binds to it. Idempotent per name: an in-progress draft is returned as-is
(the caller routes into resume), a live agent's name yields 409. Operator-only (``require_user``).

The fleet's live state right now: composition, capacity, backlog, reachability, version mix.

A read that POSTs because its agent facet is a list. ``agent_ids`` omitted means every agent the
caller may read; an empty list is an empty selection and returns zeros. There is no
``window_days`` — this is state, not flow — and posting one is a 422 rather than a silent
no-op.

What this provides that polling the agents list cannot: channel reachability, the SDK version
mix, and replica counts narrowed to the primary dual-deploy arm. Three consequences worth
knowing at the call site. ``live_replicas`` counts only heartbeat-fresh primary replicas, so it
will not equal the sum of the list's ``instances_total``; ``active_runs`` can exceed
``busy_replicas``, because a dead pod can still own a claimed run; and reachability is
agent-level and **arm-blind**, so a shadow-only-live agent reads reachable beside 0 live primary
replicas. Reachability covers heartbeat-online agents only — an offline agent is not
unreachable, it is offline, and already counted as such in the composition.

trigger was not — never 200 for a trigger that does not exist.

(its behavior is the pinned catalog image, so no route edits it), and a draft 409s — see

worker allowlist — in one idempotent call.

**Merge-patch, which is why this is a PATCH and not a PUT.** A field present in the body is
applied whole; a field absent is left untouched, so a caller may send a one-field delta and two
owners may manage different fields without clobbering each other. ``mcpGroupId`` is the one field
where absent and ``null`` differ: absent leaves the group, ``null`` unbinds it. Credential
bindings are ensure-present — the listed credentials are bound and none are unbound (unbinding
stays ``DELETE /credentials/{id}/bindings/{agent_id}``).

Re-sending the same body converges on the same state, so this is what a reconciler, a repair
after a partial apply, or an edit re-applies against. It never touches the agent's worker token.

additionally needs ``authorization.role.assign`` and ``credentialIds`` needs

the field, with nothing applied. Returns 200 when every declared field landed and 207 when some
did not, never a plain success for a field that failed.

409 draft) — a catalog agent is refused because both arms would run the same pinned image, so the
comparison a shadow exists for could not tell them apart.

declared-config route, and also 404 while the temporary ``shadow_deploy`` flag is off (both must

primary mint (``POST /worker-token``, also ``AGENT_CREATE``), not an ordinary config update, so it
carries the same ``sensitivity="high", is_admin_verb=True`` as that route and ``AGENT_REVOKE_TOKEN``
(see ``components/control/spec.py``). The plaintext token + hint are returned once — never
retrievable again, matching ``create_worker_token``/``create_agent``. Audited under the same

post.description:
Read what a document offers, before any row exists.

Persists nothing, and compiles over **every** operation so the operator picks from the whole
inventory. Gated on the configure capability rather than a read one: it makes the control plane
fetch a tenant-supplied URL on the caller's behalf.

Create the integration whole: server row, compiled document, probe override and credential
binding in one transaction.

A create-then-configure pair would leave an enabled row whose ``url`` is a JSON document, which
the catalog would dial as MCP the moment it saw it.

Read what an address advertises, before any server row exists.

This is what lets the operator find out whether they typed the URL correctly, and which tools
the server offers, without first creating a record they may have to delete. It also names the
tool the real test would validate with, so the two never disagree.

**What it can and cannot conclude.** With no credential supplied it speaks only to the
address: a server that requires auth answers identically whether the caller's credential is
good, bad or absent. Supply the one selected in the form and it is resolved for real, so a
reachable answer then does mean that credential was accepted. Gateway OAuth is the exception
either way — its token is keyed to a server that does not exist yet. It returns its own shape
rather than a ``ServerTestResponse`` so a partial answer can never be read as the full
two-layer verdict.

Egress: dialling an address of the caller's choosing adds no surface, because any caller who
may create a server can already do exactly that and then test it — and a public-URL
restriction would reject the private upstreams an Outpost binding exists to reach. Attaching a
stored credential to that dial is a different matter and carries its own, higher capability
check below.

put.description:
Re-fetch, re-compile against the new selection, and write both tables.

**The single writer** of the configuration and the compiled document, which is what removes any
race between a refresh and a configure. It re-fetches rather than re-trimming a stored original,
so editing a note needs the document's host reachable, the same fetch refresh performs, and the
already-published names are pinned across that fetch exactly as refresh pins them: otherwise
ticking one extra operation would silently rename every tool whose ``operationId`` moved
upstream since the last write.

put.description:
Route this upstream's egress through an Outpost's tunnel instead of dialing it from our pod.

Under ``mcp_server.manage`` rather than a capability of its own: this changes *where* a server is
reached from, which is the same class of change as editing its URL, and no credential is involved.

post.description:
Prove the upstream is usable, in two independently-reported layers.

Connectivity (handshake + ``list_tools``) says the transport and the credential's *shape* are
right. It does not say the credential is permitted to do anything: an under-scoped token
lists the whole tool surface and then fails on first real use, which is what made a green
test connection misleading. So a second check invokes one designated read-only tool for real.

Both layers share a single session — the deep check costs one extra round trip, not a second
handshake — and every failure is classified here, where the exception is, rather than by the
browser guessing from an error string.

Unlike the sibling introspection routes, this one deliberately surfaces the upstream's own
error text: an operator testing a connection is exactly who needs to see it.

delete.description:
Drop this install's claim, because the resource it named is gone.

The **only** thing that reaps a dangling ownership row. ``resource_id`` is polymorphic across eight
tables so it carries no foreign key, and nothing releases a claim when the resource is deleted, so a
row outlives its resource with no backstop: an age-based prune over ``claimed_at`` would unmanage
every resource older than the window rather than only the gone ones. Distinguishing the two needs
the resync's 404, which only the operator sees.

Nothing to release is a **404**, and that is a deliberate second reason rather than only an HTTP
nicety: this route is gated on an audited mutation capability, so a 2xx that released nothing earns
a baseline ``cluster_install.update`` audit row — one per no-op release, on a call a resync makes
per resource. A caller racing another replica reads 404 the same way it reads 204: the claim is
gone. A claim held by *another* install is a 409, because that caller's view is stale and silently
succeeding would hide it.

get.description:
Does this install declare this resource, and if not, who does?

The read a reconciler makes when it finds a resource by natural key with no recorded id — the state
a pod that died between a create and its status write comes back to. It separates "I created this
and lost the id", where the claim committed with the create and the resource is recoverable, from
"a human made this", where *conflict, never adopt* is the answer. Without the distinction both
collapse onto the safe branch and the operator's own resource stays conflicted until someone
deletes it by hand.

Gated on the update capability rather than ``CLUSTER_INSTALL_READ``, which an install is
deliberately not granted: that capability also lists and reads *every* install in the account, so
holding it would widen a machine credential well past the one row it is asking about. A GET behind
a mutation capability writes no audit row (the finalizer's baseline is mutations only), which this
route depends on — a reconciler asks per resource.

post.description:
Declare a resource this install did not create.

A create records its own claim inside its own transaction, so this is not that path — it is the
remaining cases: re-stating a claim whose cluster coordinates moved, and taking over a row whose
owning install is gone (which the read side already reports as unenforced, so leaving it would be a
resource no cluster can declare and nothing reaps). A row held by a **live** install is a 409 and
nothing is written: never adopt.

The install is the caller's own, never a body field — the same rule as ``self/sync``.

The install reporting that it finished a reconcile pass.

``self`` is not a placeholder for an id the caller could supply — **the install is resolved from
the credential**, which is the confused-deputy boundary ``require_outpost`` documents: an install
that could name its own id could name another one, and stamping a sync on someone else's install
would silently mask a dead operator as live. A caller that resolves to no install (every human)
gets a 404 here rather than an ability to write one.

One row per install, not one per resource, and the two columns it rewrites are unindexed on a table
with fillfactor headroom — see ``tests/test_worker_instances_hot_updates.py``.

Issue a new credential and revoke the old one. The install stops reconciling until it is
redeployed with the new value, which is why this is its own capability at the highest bar here.

Stop reconciling, and unlock UI/API editing of the resources **this** install owns.

Resuming reasserts declared state and therefore reverts whatever was edited while paused. That has to
be said in the UI rather than learned by losing a change.

get.description:
The runs of this workspace, most recent first.

All filters are optional and each selects a different relation:

- ``agent_id`` — only the runs of that one agent.
- ``q`` — free text, matched case-insensitively as a literal substring against the run id, the
  run's title (its output title, else the prompt it started from), and the display name or slug
  of the agent that ran it. It searches the **whole account**, not just the newest ``limit``
  runs, which is what lets a search find a run older than one page. ``status`` narrows to one
  run status. Both compose with the filters above and with each other.
- ``thread_id`` — the continuation chain of one conversation thread, returned whole and ordered
  **oldest-first**, so the turns read in the order they happened. This is the one mode ``limit``
  does not apply to: a thread is bounded by its own length.
- ``parent_run_id`` — the runs that run delegated to (its child runs, as recorded on each child's
  ``parent_run_id``). Ordered **newest-first**, like the unfiltered list: a delegation fan-out is
  a set of sibling runs rather than a sequence, so it carries no reading order of its own.
- ``comparison_pair_id`` — the runs of one dual-deploy comparison pair (both arms of the same
  request), newest-first.
- ``limit`` — how many runs to return, 1 to 500 (default 100).

``thread_id`` and ``parent_run_id`` select unrelated relations — one continuation, one
delegation — so asking for both at once is rejected with a ``400`` rather than intersected. A
combination that matched nothing would be indistinguishable from a genuinely empty answer.

Two properties of the result to plan for:

- **The result is capped at ``limit``, and truncation is not signalled.** A fan-out or a
  workspace with more runs than ``limit`` comes back silently short, and because the order is
  newest-first the runs left out are the oldest ones. A consumer that needs to know whether it
  saw everything must compare the number of runs returned against ``limit`` itself.
- **Large ``input``/``output`` payloads are abbreviated.** In every mode except ``thread_id``, a
  run whose ``input`` or ``output`` exceeds the list's size bound is returned as a short excerpt
  of the prompt, or the output's title, instead of the full payload. Read the run itself
  (``GET /api/v1/runs/{run_id}``) for the complete payload.

post.description:
Fleet-wide run metrics for the window: totals, the daily activity grid, model mix and the
slowest and most error-prone agents.

``window_days`` is calendar-day inclusive (``1`` is today), matching the other activity reads, and
is bounded to a year. ``agent_ids`` is an optional facet: omit the key for the whole account, or
post the ids to narrow to those agents. An **empty list narrows to nothing** and returns zeros,
which is not the same answer as omitting it.

Every quotient (``cost_per_run``, ``avg_latency_ms``, a leaderboard row's ``error_rate_pct``) is
``null`` rather than ``0`` when its denominator is empty, so a window whose runs are all still in
flight is distinguishable from one with nothing to report.

``buckets`` is dense (one entry per day of the window, zero-filled, ending today), and
``model_mix`` folds everything past the largest few models into a single ``(other)`` entry, so
both still sum to the totals.

Two costs worth knowing. The response is **five aggregate scans of the window**, which group at
four different levels and rank two ways, so nothing is shareable between them. And it aggregates
``runs``, which carries no archival flag, so account-wide totals include the runs of archived
agents while a posted facet drawn from the agent list does not.

Cancel an active run (queued/claimed/running → cancelled).

Queued cancel is exact (the run just leaves the queue). For a claimed/running run the owning worker
is also signalled to interrupt the in-flight handler; if that can't be delivered the cancel falls
back to advisory — the worker's later report is a no-op and its result is discarded.

**``cancel_signal`` says which of those happened**, because the two are indistinguishable to the
caller otherwise and only one of them means "this agent is still working". The field is additive on
a ``RunSummary``, so a client that ignores it reads exactly what it read before.

Create a new run for the same agent, seeded with the prior session snapshot.

Restoring the snapshot alone gives the agent nothing to act on; a revived run
still drives a turn with input. With no body input we reuse the original
run's input (resume a pending/failed turn); with body input we use it as the
next turn (continue a completed run).

Delivery mirrors ``/invoke``: the run is handed to the agent's live reverse SSE
channel when it has one, and otherwise left queued for the agent to claim. Either
way the snapshot is restored from the continued session, so the revived run starts
from its predecessor's state.

get.description:

targets. System-admin only; ordinary members switch among ``member_accounts`` from /auth/me
instead. Only ACTIVE accounts are returned (you can't switch into a suspended tenant), and
``limit`` is unbounded by default so the switcher pulls every active account once and resolves
any slug client-side — no silent miss for an account past a fixed cap. A positive ``limit`` still
caps the result if a caller wants to page.

post.description:
Mint a session that acts AS the target human in their account. The target becomes the effective
identity (acting with their own permissions); the originating admin is preserved in the
``impersonator_*`` claims and the action is audited.

System-admin only — enforced by the ``require_originating_system_admin`` dependency, which
re-checks live against the ORIGINATING admin, so it works from the admin's own session, from a
cross-account view, or from an existing impersonation. When a layer is already active it is exited
and re-minted onto the new target in one step (a single act-as layer at a time). The new layer's
impersonator is the originating admin, not the current effective identity, so switching who you act
as never stacks and never erases the real admin from the audit chain.

Revert an impersonation / account-view session back to the originating admin's own session.

Authorized by the signed cookie itself: only a session that carries ``impersonator_*`` claims can
call this, and it restores exactly that admin — no system-admin re-check (the effective user is
the impersonated target, which is deliberately NOT treated as admin).

Switch the active account. If the caller is a member of the target, switch to their own
principal there (ordinary org switch). Otherwise it requires a system admin, who enters via the
account's hidden ``system`` principal (cross-account view; writes flag-gated by the middleware).

Callable from within an impersonation / account-view layer: that layer is exited first and the
switch is performed from the ORIGINATING admin's own identity (re-authorized live) — seamless
rather than rejected — after which it follows the ordinary member / cross-account-view branches as
if from the admin's plain session.

post.description:
The uplink half of the envelope wire: a worker POSTs one frame, and gets one back if it asked.

**Additive.** Every existing worker→CP route keeps working untouched; this adds the envelope-shaped
path beside them. Nothing is migrated onto it here — the first user is `ping`, which exists to prove
the round trip rather than to serve a feature.

**The body is read and validated here rather than declared as a `Frame` parameter, and that is a
contract decision rather than a style one.** `frames.schema.json` states it outright: *frames are not
HTTP request bodies*. Declaring the envelope as a FastAPI model makes it one — it lands in the OpenAPI
document, and from there in every generated client, which is a second, divergent definition of the
wire contract that `agentops_rpc.wire` already owns.

It is also not merely theoretical. `Frame` carries a `not` clause (the `needsReply`/`correlationId`
exclusion), which `openapi-python-client` cannot parse; when the envelope was a declared model, that
parse failure cascaded and **silently dropped an unrelated endpoint** —
`POST /api/v1/runs/{run_id}/events` stopped being generated at all. An additive change to the frame
contract must not be able to delete somebody else's client method.

**Two status codes, because there are two outcomes and conflating them loses information.** 200 with
a frame body means "here is your answer"; 202 with no body means "accepted, nothing was owed". A
single 200-with-empty-body would make "the peer had no handler" indistinguishable from "the peer
answered with nothing", which is the distinction the S7 split exists to preserve.

Validation is therefore explicit, in two steps that fail the same way: the envelope must parse
(`Frame` sets `extra="forbid"`, so an unknown envelope field is rejected — the closed envelope stays
closed), and it must satisfy the exclusion no generated model can express.

200.description: The reply frame, when one was owed.

202.description: Accepted; the frame owed no reply.

get.description:
Queued-run count for this worker's own agent — polled by external autoscalers (e.g. KEDA's
metrics-api scaler) rather than anything in-cluster, so it's a plain worker-authenticated GET.

The ``agent_id`` query param is this route's auth-off fallback, mirroring the frame path's

get.description:
Begin the OIDC Authorization Code + PKCE flow.

With ``silent=1`` the authorize request carries ``prompt=none``: the IdP reuses an existing
SSO session and redirects straight back with a code (no login UI), or — when no live SSO
session exists — returns ``error=login_required`` to the callback, which then falls back to an
interactive login. This is how a control-plane session (a hard-capped signed cookie, no refresh
token) is transparently renewed against the longer-lived IdP session.

post.description:
Exchange a human-bound API key for the same signed session cookie the OIDC callback issues.

This is the non-interactive login path: a key minted with ``apikey mint --user-email`` acts as a
human's per-account principal, so we mint that user's session directly — no Auth0 browser
redirect. It's how the localhost-only Claude Code preview (and automated UI tests) log in as a
real user. No privilege escalation: the bearer already grants full API access as that principal;
this just additionally enables the browser/UI surface for the *same* identity.

Requires ``Authorization: Bearer <api-key>``. The key must be bound to a ``human`` principal —
a plain ``service_account`` key has no user to represent and is rejected (400).

get.description:
Login entry point.

The SPA's RequireAuth redirects here when the session is missing/expired, so the client
doesn't need to construct the provider login URL itself: this 302s to a *silent* OIDC login
(``/auth/oidc/login?silent=1``) via ``login_path``, preserving ``next``. A live IdP SSO session
is then renewed with no UI; if there is none, the callback falls back to an interactive login.
When auth is disabled (local dev) there is nothing to log into → bounce home.
